messages.content:
Chapter 1
Fear laid a heavy fog over the boys as the bus rolled toward the guard gate at Marine Corps Recruit Depot, Parris Island. The lights illuminated a sign that read WELCOME TO PARRIS ISLAND. WE MAKE MARINES.
The boys aboard the bus had come from all walks of life and all parts of the eastern United States. Some had a history of Marine Corps service in their family. Some had a desire to serve their country and they wanted to fight with the best. Others were out of options. Attending college was out of the question, due to either lack of funds or desire. They had no prospects in the workforce. They were heading down a path of self-destruction and needed a way out that avoided jail time. All of them wanted to be Marines and most of them would make it.
The bus drove down the road that cut through the South Carolina swamp. The only road on or off Parris Island. Civilian life was being left behind. The bus navigated the narrow streets of the recruit depot. The driver had made this trip many times before. The bus turned a corner and as they approached the receiving building one of the recruits broke the silence.
“There’s the yellow footprints.”
Many of the recruits looked out of the windows to see the footprints. The bus stopped in its designated spot alongside them. On the opposite side of the bus, several recruits stood and looked over the heads to take in the sight of the footprints themselves.
“Ah hell,” said a recruit, when he saw the drill instructors walking toward the bus. “They’re coming.”
Quiet murmurs began with instructions for fellow recruits to sit down. 
The drill instructors were dressed in their Service C uniforms. Crisp tan shirt with award ribbons. Perfectly pressed olive drab trousers. Green drill belt. Black Oxford high gloss dress shoes. And the drill instructor identifier, the campaign cover (aka Smokey Bear) perfectly perched on their heads. The three DIs walked with such precision and determination. As each step brought them closer to the bus, the recruits' heart rates increased. All eyes were on the lead drill instructor as he boarded the silent bus.
“Sit up straight right now! Put your heels together and look straight ahead!” The drill instructor snapped. 
 The bus rocked at the sudden shift made by the recruits. These were the first instructions that a drill instructor would give to them. The drill instructor continued his instructions, slowly and deliberately moving down the aisle.
“Now when I tell you to, you’re gonna grab everything you brought on this bus with you including the trash that you made. You’re gonna get up. You’re gonna exit the bus. You’re gonna get on the yellow footprints out there. Do you understand that!”
He had spoken with such speed and in a tone that many of them had never heard before. Some answered with understanding. They were the prepared ones, the ones who had family members in the Corps or who had listened to the guidance of their recruiter or who had watched videos on YouTube about what to expect at Marine Corps boot camp.
The ones who could muster a sound said, “Yes, sir.”
This response was not acceptable to the drill instructor. The new recruits would soon find out that most of what they said and did would not be acceptable to any DI.
“I said, do you understand that!” The DI’s voice had not become louder, but had become more intense.
“Yes, sir!” Most of the recruits increased their volume, hoping to impress the drill instructor, but because they would not see each other again after the next few days, this was in vain. The recruits would learn that they will meet several new drill instructors before being introduced to the men who would transform them into Marines. Other recruits believed they were too cool to join the suck up platoon, so they let their initial response stand on its own.
The DI turned around and walked to the front of the bus, where he had boarded. He turned and faced the recruits.
“Get up! Get off my bus!”
The frightened recruits moved as quickly as they believed they could, grabbing the few personal items they had brought with them. This mostly consisted of the items they were wearing, a few Bibles and paperwork they had been given before they boarded the bus. The cool recruits moved slowly in their belief that the drill instructors had no real power and that the recruits would be able to walk through life the way they had done up to that point. They would later learn that on Parris Island, their actions had consequences. 
The drill instructor continued screaming, “Get off my bus! Get up! Move!” 
Most of the remaining recruits shot up out of their seats and made a beeline down the aisle of the bus and down the steps through the door. They were greeted by more drill instructors who were screaming the order to get on the yellow footprints. The DIs directed the recruits to the footprints, not by pointing the way, but by leaning in with their bodies and pushing with the heat of their voices. The first recruit fumbled his way to the yellow footprints, not sure which one to stand on. There were 18 rows of 4 and for some reason he chose to stand on the third footprint of the second row. Fortunately for him, the recruits that followed filled the spots ahead of and behind him. His mistake had gone unnoticed. 
Back on the bus, the first drill instructor moved in with swiftness on the recruits who were having trouble grasping the concept of speed. He zeroed in on a recruit who had yet to stand up from his seat. He was either too cool or too ignorant to get it.
The drill instructor leaned into the face of the recruit close enough for the recruit to feel the heat emanating from the drill instructor’s forehead. 
The DI began screaming, “Get uuup! Get! Off! My! Bus!” His spit sprayed in short spurts at the end of every word. “Get uuup!”
The recruit snapped out of his daze, “Yes, Sir!” and sprung to his feet.
The DI stepped back and the recruit bolted from his seat, out of the bus and to his spot with his fellow recruits. After a loud quick 30 seconds, all of the recruits were off the bus and standing on a pair of yellow footprints. Silent and scared. Sweating through their polo shirt or button down. Even though it was the middle of the night and only 81 degrees, the humidity on Parris Island was opening up new pores.
The drill instructors were not immune to this South Carolina swamp characteristic. Some of them had been onboard the island for nearly a year yet all of their uniforms were wet with sweat. Some of the recruits were breathing heavily after the short brisk move from the bus to the footprints. Their stamina would need to increase if they planned on making it to the eagle, globe, and anchor ceremony at the end of the third phase of training.
The bus pulled away, taking their civilian life with it.
 It was a haze of the mind and the recruits could not tell which one of the drill instructors had instructed them to get off the bus and onto his yellow footprints. One of the drill instructors addressed the recruits from their left side. His voice carried the same raspy tone that commanded immediate respect. He walked back and forth along the left side of the formation of recruits as he gave his well rehearsed speech.
“You are now aboard Marine Corps Recruit Depot, Parris Island, South Carolina and you have just taken the first step toward becoming a member of the world’s finest fighting force, The United States Marine Corps. You should be standing at the position of attention. That means your heels are touching, your feet are at a forty-five degree angle, palms drawn inboard, fingers curled under, your thumbs are on your trouser seams and your head and eyes are straight to the front. And your mouth is shut.”
As the DI gave his instructions on the position of attention, several of the recruits looked down to see that their feet were in the proper position. They would soon find out that every movement made in a platoon at attention is noticed.
The DI went on to explain to the recruits that they were now required to live by the Uniform Code of Military Justice as well as by civilian laws.
The DI continued, “To your right is the receiving building. Here you will meet your receiving drill instructors who will be with you for the next 3 to 5 days. After which, you will be turned over to a team of drill instructors who will train you over the next 12 weeks. Do we understand?”
“Yes, Sir!”
“You will do what you are told to do when you are told to do it. Without question! Do we understand!”
“Yes, Sir!”
“Starting now, you will work as a team. You will live, eat, sleep and train as a team. The word ‘I’ will no longer be a part of your vocabulary. Do we understand?”
“Yes, Sir!”
“Tens of thousands of Marines began outstanding service to our country on the very footprints where you are standing. You will carry on their proud tradition.”
The drill instructor let that sink in for a brief moment. That simple group of 72 stenciled non-descripped yellow footprints had been the starting point of thousands and thousands of Marines since 1965 when the footprints were first installed. Some of those Marines were still living, others died in the jungles of South Vietnam mere months after standing on those painted footprints. 
“Now, when I tell you to, you will form four straight lines, side by side in front of my silver hatches at the bottom of the steps.”
The DI pointed with a flat-palmed open hand to two large silver doors at the front of the brick receiving building. That gesture is called a knife hand and it is employed heavily by Marine Corps drill instructors. That was the first of many knife hands these recruits would encounter. 
“Do we understand?”
“Yes, Sir!”
“OK! Do we understand!”
“Yes, Sir!”
“You will walk fast. You will not run. Do we understand?”
“Yes, Sir!”
“Get over there now!”
“Yes, Sir!”
The recruits stuttered forward then began walking a few steps. The DI started counting down from 20. The recruits picked up the pace of their walk, trying to not run. Squeaking their shoes along the brick walkway.
“Sixteen, fifteen, thirteen, twelve, eleven, nine…” Drill instructors have a habit of skipping numbers when counting down and changing the pace at which they count. This serves as one of the methods to get recruits to move as fast they can when executing a command. 
The recruits finished filing into their spots, staying behind the recruit they were behind on the yellow footprints.
“Hurry up! Five, four, three, two, and… ONE!”
“Done sir!” The recruits announced that they had completed successfully the task which they had been assigned. 
The DI instructed them to button their shirts to the top, unroll their long sleeves and button the cuffs. He counted them down from 30, which took about 15 seconds. They continued standing at attention with their paperwork under their arms. 
Marine Corps drill instructors are special characters who use exaggerated movements, knife hands, threatening looks, and loud frog like raspy voices to instill fear in recruits. The DI who addressed these new recruits deployed and executed at will as he performed his next speech.
“Standing before you are two silver hatches. These silver hatches signify your transformation from a civilian to a United States Marine Corps recruit. Therefore you will pass through these hatches once and never again! Do we understand!”
“Yes, Sir!”
The DI was not pleased with the recruits’ volume. “Scream, yes, Sir!”
“Yes, Sir!”
With double clenched fists and extended index fingers, the drill instructor pointed at two recruits in the front of the formation.
“You two, get up here.” 
“Yes, Sir!”
He directed them to the top of the stairs with such force they felt as if they were being pulled against their will.
“Say aye sir when I tell you to do something. Do you understand me?”
“Yes, Sir!”
The recruits stopped at the top of the steps and awaited instruction that came almost immediately. 
“Open my silver hatches.” 
“Aye, Sir!” The two recruits grabbed the handles, pulled the silver hatches open, and stood to the side like doormen.
The DI stepped to the side and addressed the recruits at the bottom of the steps. “All you get in right now!”
“Aye, Sir!” The platoon of recruits moved quickly
“Scream aye sir!” 
“Aye, Sir!” The recruits screamed as they rushed in through the silver hatches and were met by three more screaming DIs who were instructing them on where to go next.
“Move faster, right now!”
“Aye, Sir!” The recruits moved like frightened cattle, followed the head in front of them and tried to understand the wild hand gestures and screaming guidance of the drill instructors.
“Get over there right now! Sit down right now! “Open your mouth right now!”
“Aye, Sir!”
One by one in quick succession, each recruit stopped next to one of the permanently affixed desks made of stainless steel and wood. They were ordered to stand at attention and wait for the command to sit.
All of the recruits were in position and the drill instructors had taken their places. The DI at the front of the room took control.
“Sit down right now!”
Only a few of the recruits responded with the appropriate aye sir while all of the recruits sat at their desks.
“OK! Stand up right now!” The drill instructor was angered by the recruits’ lack of response to his command. 
The recruits stood up. “Aye, Sir!”
“Sit down right now!”
They sat down.
“Aye, Sir!”
“Stand up right now!” The DI was messing with them, a common tactic of the Marine Corps Drill Instructor.
“Aye, Sir!” They remained standing. 
“You will do what you are told to do when you are told to do it! And you will answer ‘aye sir.’ Do you understand!”
“Yes, Sir!”
“Sit down right now!”
“Aye, Sir!” The recruits sat.
Sitting, while necessary, was dangerous because many of the recruits had been awake for more than 20 hours at that point, and the next time they’d get to lie down in a bed would be in 36 hours. By then, it would be called a rack.


Chapter 2
The recruits had finished their initial paperwork and it was time to continue with the receiving process. The drill instructor who had guided them ever so gently through the paperwork, instructed them further.
“Stand up right now!”
“Aye, Sir!” 
The recruits stood quickly. One faltered. His leg had fallen asleep. He sat back down then stood after realizing his mistake. It was too late. He’d been targeted. It was a good thing for him that these DIs were not going to be his training DIs. One mistake in the beginning could highlight a recruit’s faults for the rest of the cycle. 
“I don’t think so, Bambi!” The DI rushed to the side of the recruit who was favoring his tingling leg. The DI arrived with a raised knife hand and a scowl on his face. He looked directly into the recruit’s wide, frightened eyes. The brim of his Smokey Bear was pressing into Bambi’s forehead.
“Sit!” A direct command given to Bambi, whose real name was Jensen. Michael Ray Jensen. 
“Aye, Sir!” Jensen sat.
***
Recruit Jensen’s frame was in direct contrast to his new nickname. However, the DI had no idea of the similarities in the stories of Jensen and his namesake. Just like Bambi of the forest, Jensen’s mother had been killed by a hunter. Not a hunter in the forest, but a hunter in the streets. Jensen’s neighborhood had been under the control of street gangs since before he was born. His mother had been caught in the crossfire of a driveby shooting when Jensen was 15 years old. Destiny Jensen was 29 years old. It was learned that the shooter of the lethal rounds was 15 years old too and a classmate of Jensen’s. 
The shooter, Calvin Bishop, turned himself in after becoming violently ill with guilt the night of the shooting. He told the judge it was an accident, he had never meant to shoot Miss Jensen. He liked her. She had given him cookies when he was a kid. The judge sentenced him to serve 3 years in a youth detention center in Georgia, after which time the boy moved to a different part of the state, a few hours from Valdosta where Jensen had grown up.
Jensen never knew the guy who had gotten his mom pregnant and then split, like so many other black dads. He would never refer to him as his dad. 
***
“Now, the rest of you,” said a DI by the hallway, “starting with this row right here,” he pointed with a clenched fist and pointed index finger, “will follow me to the phone bank where you will call your mommy and tell her you’re okay. You will only say what is written on the paper at the phone. You will not say anything else! Do you understand!”
“Yes, Sir!”
“Scream yes sir!”
“Yes, Sir!”
“Move!”
The first row of new recruits followed him down the hallway. The other rows fell in behind. A recruit near the end looked back at Jensen and said a silent prayer for him, then himself. Recruit Barnett faced front and continued down the hall. Jensen was left behind with a swarm of DIs who instructed him, for the next 20 minutes, on the proper way to sit and stand. 
At the bank of telephones, Jensen was finally allowed to make his call home. What home? he thought. 
All the other recruits had moved on in the processing sequence and were loading gear into their new government issued green sea bags. Everything they would need was being issued to them. Underwear (skivvies), soap, batteries for their moon beam (flashlight), canteens, socks, t-shirts, green and desert utility uniforms (cammies), sewing kit, hygiene gear, tennis shoes (go fasters), 8 point covers (utility uniform hats), glow in the dark belts for physical training, etcetera.
“Okay, Bambi, call your mommy.” said the DI who was still with Jensen. 
Jensen was feeling a tad angry and disrespectful after his 20 minutes of private instruction. He had been on the island for about an hour and he already felt regret about his decision. He wondered how he could make it if the rest of his time on the island was like what he’d experienced so far.
“My mom’s dead,” he said without emotion. He had put the experience behind him about a year prior. He had to.
The DI was not affected by this news. He had heard it many times before from other recruits. Mom’s dead. Dad’s dead. Grandparents raised me, but they’re dead. Just call somebody then, thought the DI. It doesn’t matter to me.
“Then I guess you better call your daddy.”
“Don’t know him,” Jensen said, standing at attention, staring at the phone on the wall. 
The DI bit his lower lip, raised a knife hand to Jensen’s face, leaned in pressing his Smokey Bear brim against his forehead again, and said, “Bambi, pick up that freakin phone and call somebody who would care if you were dead. I don’t care if it’s your boo, your auntie, your dealer or your pastor. Call somebody now!”
“Aye, Sir!”
Jensen snatched the phone off the wall and thought quickly about who to call. He had thought he could skip calling since he believed there was no one who cared that he had left Valdosta. Maybe Mrs. Baker, he thought.
***
Mrs. Baker had been Jensen’s high school English teacher. She had taken him under her wing during his junior year and helped him through a difficult time. Before she intervened, his life had been heading the way of the kid who had shot his mom. Mrs. Baker had shown him how to work through problems by journaling. Journaling turned into writing poetry, short stories and a prize winning essay in his senior year. His favorite writing, though, was a poem about his mom’s death and his thoughts afterwards.
Young life taken by a gun
Left behind an only son
Raised to know right from wrong
Down a slippery slope before too long
Feeling lonely and shunned by society
A gang could be my family
***
He believed Mrs. Baker had saved his life, but that she was only doing her civic duty as a teacher. Jensen had never told her that. He had her phone number memorized, just in case. She had given it to him and told him to call anytime he needed anything. He had called her a few times before, but never in the middle of the night. What time is it anyway? he thought.
Jensen placed the phone receiver to his ear and dialed Mrs. Baker’s number. He looked at the script on the wall and read it in his mind while the phone rang on the other end. After six rings, she answered.
“Hello?” She sounded groggy and a little hoarse. 
Jensen was surprised that she answered and this caused him to stumble over his words even though he was reading from a script that was pasted on the phone box.
“Th--this is Mich--this is Recruit Jensen. I have arrived safely at Parris Island. Please do not send any food or bulky items to me in the mail. I will contact you in seven to nine days by letter with my new address. Thank you for your support. Goodbye for now.”
Although the phone call had been void of all emotion and connection, it felt natural to Jensen whose last close relationship was with his mom. He believed his relationship with Mrs. Baker was purely educational and that she had no interest in mailing him anything at all. He would not be sending her his address.
As a natural reaction, Jensen held the phone to his ear for a moment.
“Michael?” said Mrs. Baker.
“Hang up, Bambi! You’re done!”
“Aye, Sir!” Jensen hung up the receiver.
***
Kylie Baker pulled the phone away from her ear and looked at the screen.
“Who was that?” asked her husband, Jason, as he leaned up on his elbow to look over Kylie’s shoulder. 
She continued looking at her phone for a moment and then laid it back down on her nightstand. She turned over to face Jason and propped herself up on her elbow, matching him.
“I think it was Mike Jensen.”
“Who?”
“You know, Mike Jensen, the kid whose mom was killed several years ago.”
Jason nodded trying to remember, then said, “Right, right. What did he want? To be bailed out or something?”
Kylie let out an exasperated sigh and shook her head. “No, and that’s not fair either.”
“Sorry, it’s the middle of the night and-”
Kylie interrupted him because she knew where his head was. “And he’s a black (NOTE: maybe African American should be said–but it doesn't sound like how people talk) kid who doesn’t have any parents, so of course he’s calling from jail, right?”
“I don’t know,” said Jason shrugging his shoulder, knowing there was no way out of what he had already said. 
She sighed. “I think he was calling from boot camp.”
“Boot camp?”
“Yeah, I didn’t catch much of what he said, but I know he said he arrived at Parris Island.”
“Parris Island, huh. That’s the Marines, right?
“I’m fairly certain,” she said.
“Why did he call you?” Jason asked. 
“I don’t know,” she said as she laid back down, resting her head on her pillow.
Jason sat up in the bed and shifted to look straight at Keli. Concern in his eyes.
She continued, “Maybe because he doesn’t have any parents. Maybe my work finally means something to one of those kids.”


Chapter 3
By the time Jensen caught up with the platoon, they were receiving their first of many regulation haircuts. The recruits were standing at the position of attention in a single file line along the wall of windows. There were three barber’s chairs evenly spaced in front of a row of cabinets with sink basins.
“Next,” said the barber.
The next recruit stepped forward to the chair and sat straight up with his hands palm down, flat on his thighs. His eyes were wide open. He had a Jonas Brothers haircut that had taken him a full year to grow, style and perfect. The barber turned on his clippers.
“Relax your head. It’s only a haircut,” he said.
The barber placed his left hand on top of the recruit’s head and tilted it back a few degrees. He laid the steel blades of the clipper on the recruit’s forehead and slid them through his thick dark brown hair. In less than 60 seconds, his locks were gone and he looked the same as the 27 recruits who had, so far, contributed to the pile of hair being swept up and thrown away.
***
After a day and a half of no sleep and non-stop yelling and instruction, Jensen and his platoon were finally in their temporary squad bay standing in their shower shoes, heels on a black line that ran the length of the bay. The receiving drill instructor was instructing them on how they would be sleeping.
“You will lie down in the position of attention on top of your green blanket until you are given permission to adjust. When you are given permission to adjust, you may cover up your nasty body with your sheet and blanket. Do you understand!”
“Yes, Sir!”
“Scream yes sir!”
“Yes, Sir!”
“When I say move, you will move to the rack and lay down! Do you understand!”
“Yes, Sir!”
“Move!”
“Aye, Sir!”
The recruits were exhausted and ready for sleep yet they moved with speed to their racks and laid down.
Jensen was lying at the position of attention waiting for the command to adjust. He began to doze off immediately and awoke briefly at the sound of the DI’s voice.
“A--djust!”
Jensen fell asleep at the position of attention, on top of his blanket. He was awakened in what seemed like the blink of an eye by the sound of banging trash can lids and someone screaming.
“Lights, lights, lights! Get up! Get out of the rack! Get on the line now! Move! Move! Move!”
Jensen popped up and planted his feet on the deck. He stood, but his leg was asleep again and this forced him to sit on the bed. Jensen saw the drill instructor barreling down the center of the squad bay (aka, the highway) and knew he needed to get up and get on the line. Jensen stood again, but his leg was still asleep. He hobbled to the line and the DI saw it all. He swooped in and Jensen felt the wind push against him. The DI moved in closer and executed a move that Jensen was all too familiar with, the Smokey Bear brim against his forehead.
“What’s your problem!” The DI yelled at an alarming level.
Jensen sensed that the DI cared less about Jensen’s problem than about, well anything. He was hoping that he’d get let off the hook since he had no control over when his leg fell asleep.
“My leg is asleep, sir.”
“My! My! I guess we just say ‘my’ now! How bout ‘this recruit’!”
Jensen was still trying to learn the new vocabulary he’d been taught. No ‘I’. No ‘my’. No ‘me’. No ‘you’. Only ‘this recruit’, ‘that recruit’.
“Yes, Sir! This recruit’s leg is asleep, Sir!”
“Oh, you must be Bambi! Do you got a gimp leg, Bambi! How’d you get onto my island, Bambi!”
Jensen hoped that Bambi would die during receiving. He held his response because there were multiple questions in the air and he was confused on which to answer.
“Well, Bambi! Open! Your! Mouth!”
“Aye, Sir!” He could think of nothing else to say. 
“Aye, Sir, what!”
Jensen had no idea what to say. He had just been awakened from well needed sleep by the banging of a trash can on the floor while somebody was yelling at the top of their lungs.
“I don’t know, sir!”
Oh no, thought Jensen.
“I! I! Are you retarded, Bambi!”
“No, Sir! This recruit is not retarded, Sir!”
“Then get on the line!”
The drill instructor broke away and started counting down from 15 before Jensen could speak.
“Aye, Sir!” Jensen straightened his posture and looked down to ensure his heels were on the line. His leg was awake now. He looked across the highway and saw that the other recruits had their shower shoes on. He thought for a split second that he should go get his shower shoes from under his rack, but decided against it, hoping it would go unnoticed. 
“And...one!”
“Done, Sir, done!” The recruits said in near unison.
***
Jensen spent the remaining two days of receiving with the same drill instructors who continued to call him Bambi. He had a feeling that this nickname was going to stick with him throughout bootcamp. It was growing on him even though he would prefer a different one. In a funny way, the nickname made him feel wanted, remembered. He realized how he had missed being remembered. He thought of Mrs. Baker and wondered if she figured out what the call was all about. That phone call was the first anyone had heard about his joining the Marine Corps.
“Let’s go, Bambi, you’re up!” said the drill instructor in front of the pull-up bars. 
Jensen’s platoon was conducting their initial strength test to ensure that each recruit was physically fit to begin training. He had no concerns that he’d be able to meet the requirements. In order to stay out of trouble he had spent his spare time running and exercising. 
“Aye, Sir!” Jensen stepped up to the bar and stood at attention.
“Sir, Recruit Jensen requests permission to mount the bar, Sir!”
“Mount the bar,” said a DI.
“Aye, Sir!” Jensen jumped up a few inches and grabbed hold of the pull-up bar.
The DI saw that Jensen had mounted the bar and was waiting.
“Begin!” 
“Aye, Sir!” Jensen began his pull-ups while Recruit Hayes counted each repetition.
“One!...Two!...Three!...”
“Count when he comes down! That’s two,” said the DI.
Jensen continued the pull-ups.
“Aye, Sir! Three!...” continued Hayes, “Four!...Five!”
“All the way down, Bambi!”
“Aye, Sir!”
“Seven!...Eight!...Nine!”
Jensen was feeling strong and accomplished.
“Eleven!...Twelve!...Thirteen!”
Jensen struggled pulling up on the next one and kicked his legs out to give himself momentum.
“You’re done, Bambi!”
“Aye, Sir! Recruit Jensen requests permission to dismount the bar, Sir!”
“Dismount!”
“Aye, Sir!” Jensen dropped from the bar and ran to the ammo can lift station. When instructed to, he brought the 30 pound ammo can to shoulder height and lifted it above his head in repetitions through 68. With two successful tasks under his belt, he moved to the sit-up station where he banged out the perfect score of 100 sit-ups in 2 minutes. He followed that up with a 1.5 mile run in under 11 minutes, well below the minimum standard of 13:30.
The congratulations he received came from himself. It would be a long time before he heard any positive remarks from his drill instructors. 
Chapter 4
Recruit Jensen’s platoon was sitting Indian style in six columns of ten on the floor of the squad bay they would call home for the following twelve weeks. Their hands were opened flat, palms down and placed on their knees. Both of Jensen's legs were asleep from sitting in this position. He hoped that he'd get used to sitting this way because he had heard that recruits sit like this for hours at a time. He thought about what would happen when he stood from this position in front of his new drill instructors. He was holding out hope that his nickname had stayed in Receiving because Bambi was a wimpy name, especially for a future Marine.
The platoon looked straight ahead while the series commander, Captain Michaels, turned the recruits over to their drill instructors.
“Senior Drill Instructor, take charge of these recruits and train them to become United States Marines.”
Senior Drill Instructor Staff Sergeant Wilcox saluted Captain Michaels.
“Aye, Sir.” He dropped his salute and Captain Michaels faced left then marched off. 
Wilcox took no time before exploding into his introductions and speech.
“Sit up straight and look at me! My name is Staff Sergeant Wilcox and I am your senior drill instructor! I am assisted in my duties by Drill Instructor Sergeant McClure and Drill Instructor Sergeant Martinez. Our mission is to train each one of you to become a United States Marine! A Marine is characterized as one who possesses the highest of military virtues! He obeys orders, respects his seniors, and strives constantly to be the best at everything he does. Discipline and spirit are the hallmarks of a Marine! Each of you can become a Marine if you develop discipline and spirit. We will give every effort to train you, even after some of you have given up on yourselves.”
Chills spread across Jensen's body and he wondered if they were from the SDI’s speech or if his whole body was tingling because of the way he was sitting. Staff Sergeant Wilcox continued with the well rehearsed speech that every new recruit hears from his senior drill instructor.
“Starting now, you will treat me and all other Marines with the highest respect, for we have earned our places as Marines and will accept nothing less than that from you! We will treat you as we do our fellow Marines: with firmness, fairness, dignity and compassion. At no time will you be physically or verbally abused by any Marine or recruit. If anyone should abuse or mistreat you, I expect you to report such incidents immediately to me or one of my drill instructors. Further, if you believe that I have mistreated you, I expect you to report it to the series commander, Captain Michaels.”
There is no way I’m gonna snitch on somebody, thought Jensen. If I can’t take it, then I shouldn’t be a Marine.
“My drill instructors and I will be with you every day, everywhere you go! I have told you what my drill instructors and I will do for you. From you, we expect the following. You must give one hundred percent of yourself at all times! Obey all orders, instantly, willingly, and without question! Treat all Marines and recruits with courtesy and respect! You will not physically abuse or verbally threaten another Marine or recruit! Be completely honest in everything you do. A Marine never lies, cheats, or compromises!
